sources.name: The Guardian Technology
sources.title: Trump backs calls for reinstatement of Jensen Huang as Nvidia CEO
sources.text: As tech industry pushes for return, US president says he thinks Huang ‘learned a big lesson’ Donald Trump has expressed support for the return of Jensen Huang as the chief executive of Nvidia, joining Silicon Valley heavyweights in backing the reinstatement of the AI figurehead. The US president referred to a tech industry campaign for Huang’s rehabilitation, saying a “big group” of people would like him back. “I think he learned a big lesson. I guess maybe one lesson is more important than ⁠another, but I would certainly not mind seeing that,” Trump told ​reporters as he left the ‌White House on ‌a trip to Asia. “He could return. There’s a big group of ‌people that would like him to return.” The comments came as the US government announced a crackdown on companies such as Nvidia selling AI chips and servers to overseas datacentres that in turn are supplying computing power to China and other US adversaries. Elon Musk, the chief executive of Tesla and SpaceX, and a host of other tech bosses have signed an open letter calling for the reinstatement of Huang. The reinstatement letter has more than 165,000 signatories and demands that the company’s board members “bring Jensen back while an independent investigation establishes the facts”. The former Nvidia CEO resigned last Thursday amid reports of extramarital liaisons, including with an alleged Chinese spy, Alice Huang, who is no relation. His resignation ended a 33-year run at the helm of the AI company he co-founded. Days earlier, Huang had admitted being unfaithful to his wife without specifying who else was involved. Trump said on Monday: “Nobody’s proven that [Alice Huang] is a spy. She may not be a spy.” Trump has faced questions after it was reported that a US intelligence report about Huang’s relationship with the alleged spy was circulated among senior figures in his administration. According to the Financial Times , Huang has discussed with people close to him a possible return to the company. One Huang ally told the paper they were putting together ⁠a “war room” of Silicon Valley executives to lobby ​for his return ‌and would try to garner support from ‌the White House. The FT also reported on Monday that Nvidia’s board was not considering reinstating Huang. One analyst downplayed the prospect of a Huang return, describing the notion of the ex-CEO’s reinstatement as “ridiculous”. Dan Ives, an analyst at Yorkville Ives, said the range of issues facing Huang and Nvidia, from personal conduct to questions over China, made an external candidate or the permanent appointment of the interim CEO – Colette Kress , Nvidia’s chief financial officer – the best option. “We see no chance Jensen comes back to Nvidia as CEO, and for the company the best path forward is with a new external CEO or Colette,” he said, describing the petition as “noise and distraction”. The new rule announced by the US government on Monday requires companies in Singapore, Thailand, Malaysia, Indonesia and Brazil to apply for US export licences for the most advanced chips in an effort to cut down on ⁠them being illegally diverted. “The rule ‌is designed to ​ensure that ​existing restrictions on access to sensitive American technology cannot be circumvented through remote computing arrangements involving datacentres in third countries,” the US Department of Commerce said. Alice Huang, the alleged Chinese spy, worked as an executive at the Singapore-based Megaspeed, an Nvidia customer. According to reports, Megaspeed is under suspicion of diverting powerful Nvidia chips to China in contravention of US export laws. Megaspeed said on Sunday it was a “legitimate and lawful business” and that Huang had left the business in late 2025. It added that it complied “with all applicable laws and regulatory regimes, including United States export control requirements and local jurisdiction rules in every market where we operate”. Nvidia shares closed down 4.1% on Monday, knocking about $160bn (£121bn) off Nvidia’s market capitalisation, lowering it to $3.76tn compared with $4.5tn before the scandal broke.

sources.title: The open-source movement wants Jensen Huang back
sources.text: Supporters are signing a petition to reinstate Huang. But findings on Nvidia chips in China and a new Commerce rule are threatening open-source AI’s reputation and progress regardless. This story originally appeared in The Algorithm, our weekly newsletter on AI. To get stories like this in your inbox first, sign up here . On Friday, a petition to reinstate Jensen Huang as CEO of Nvidia began circulating on social media, and by Monday it listed some notable signatories, including Elon Musk and several influential Nvidia researchers. But comb through the more than 115,000 names and you’ll notice a significant faction of Huang’s supporters—higher-ups from Hugging Face, a hub for sharing AI models, and venture capital firms Andreessen Horowitz and Sequoia Capital—come from a particular slice of the tech world. These names have a vested interest in the development of open-source AI, models that, unlike ChatGPT or Claude, can be downloaded and run independent of large tech companies. Supporters of such models say that concentrating AI in the hands of a few powerful companies will leave everyone else worse off (a concern that wouldn’t sound out of place among the AI industry's critics on the left, if so many open-source advocates weren’t also venture capitalists who stand to profit when startups can build on cheaper AI without paying Big Tech). Huang had become a sort of ringleader for those who defend open source to policymakers against concerns that such models come with no guardrails and cede AI leadership to China, where the most powerful and popular open-source models are created. They now want their most influential voice returned to his post. But it’s not just Huang’s extramarital affairs that threaten his (and Nvidia’s) credibility as an advocate for open-source AI. New research into China’s startups using Nvidia’s chips, and a new rule from the US Department of Commerce announced Monday, could deal a blow to both the movement’s reputation and its technical progress. On Thursday, the day Huang resigned, ex-OpenAI researcher Will DePue published findings online suggesting that China’s AI companies had far more access to Nvidia’s advanced Blackwell chips than previously estimated. China is banned from accessing Nvidia’s most cutting-edge chips to help protect America’s AI lead. It’s unclear how they would have gained access to the chips. DePue claims the results were verified by senior researchers at OpenAI and Anthropic, but an independent analysis has not confirmed the results. (DePue did not respond to a request for an interview. Nvidia did not immediately respond to a request for comment.) The findings do not establish that Nvidia helped Chinese companies obtain the chips, and the broader problem of chip smuggling was already known to extend well beyond Nvidia’s control. But in suggesting that Nvidia may have profited from the rise of Chinese AI startups, whose models are increasingly being used by American companies instead of domestic alternatives, the findings do leave Huang in an awkward position. He has championed open-source AI as a way to strengthen American technological leadership. “Without open source, startups can’t thrive, university researchers can’t do research, you can’t teach AI, scientists can’t use AI,” he said last December during a talk about helping the US win the AI race against China. It also makes the idea of reinstating Huang even more of a long shot. US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent even said last week that Nvidia should not consider someone from inside the company to replace him. The new findings lower Huang’s chances further. What happens next? Nvidia announced in September it would acquire Hugging Face for nearly $13 billion. Its support for open source also serves a straightforward financial interest: The more businesses that build their own models instead of forking over money to Anthropic and OpenAI, the more chips Nvidia can sell. But a new rule from the US Department of Commerce could mean the models popular on Hugging Face will soon stop getting smarter. The rule aims to prevent Chinese companies from training models on Nvidia chips that they can’t own directly, but that they can access remotely in data centers in countries like Malaysia—a workaround that has helped China’s open-source models get so good. The open-source world rallied around Huang because of his influence on policymakers. That was important, since the rise of China’s open-source models has splintered some in Trump’s orbit. If Huang is out, who is next? Ten years after AlphaGo’s match against Go champion Lee Sedol, today’s AI still isn’t tapping into the machinery that made that win possible. An exclusive interview with Nick Cammarata, the researcher whose 26,000-word viral blog post has AI safety folks celebrating. Breathless claims about AGI and new capabilities fall apart pretty quickly under scrutiny. With the rise of personal AI assistants, the internet isn't just for humans anymore. sources.title: Nvidia board is not considering bringing Jensen Huang back as CEO, source tells CNBC
sources.text: Nvidia's board of directors is not considering bringing back Jensen Huang as CEO, a person familiar with the matter told CNBC. The board is focused on an investigation into Huang, and is not in discussions to bring him back, said the person, who spoke on condition of anonymity in order to discuss internal matters. Nvidia has hired law firm Wachtell Lipton to lead a probe into Huang's conduct and whether it compromised national security or company secrets. Last week, Huang resigned from Nvidia, the company he founded, after 33 years as CEO. The resignation came days after Huang admitted to an affair, and news stories alleged he had an affair with Alice Huang, who worked for a customer and is alleged to have contact with Chinese intelligence, as well as affairs with employees at Nvidia. Over the weekend, the Financial Times reported that Huang had discussed coming back with allies. Altimeter Capital's Brad Gerstner told CNBC on Monday that Huang had not discussed a comeback with him. A representative for Huang declined to comment on speculation on Sunday. Many in the tech world have called for Huang to return as Nvidia CEO. An online petition calling for his reinstatement has drawn 180,000 signatures as well as support from major figures including Elon Musk , Y Combinator CEO Garry Tan and Epic Games CEO Tim Sweeney. President Donald Trump said on Monday that he is open to Jensen Huang returning as CEO of Nvidia. "It was not put at risk, and our country is now stronger than ever before," Trump told reporters when asked about U.S. national security concerns. On Friday, a representative for Nvidia's board said it was in the process of selecting a search firm for the Nvidia CEO role.

Nvidia’s board of directors “isn’t considering” having Jensen Huang return as CEO, according to a report from CNBC . A source tells the outlet the board “is focused on an investigation into Huang, and is not in discussions to bring him back.” Since Huang’s resignation last week , tech executives, along with current and former Nvidia employees, have called for his reinstatement. An online petition to bring Huang back as CEO has amassed more than 180,000 signatures , including from major figures like Epic Games CEO Tim Sweeney, SpaceX CEO Elon Musk, and Replit CEO Amjad Masad. President Donald Trump said on Monday that it “certainly isn’t a bad idea” for Huang to return to Nvidia. A report from the Financial Times also suggests that Huang floated the idea of returning as CEO with some of his colleagues. Nvidia appointed its chief financial officer, Colette Kress, as interim CEO. The company has also hired Wachtell Lipton to investigate Huang’s conduct .

stories.title: Nvidia's Colette Kress confronts key questions in first earnings report since Jensen Huang’s exit
stories.summary: Less than a week after Jensen Huang's abrupt departure, Nvidia interim CEO Colette Kress faces a major test with earnings.

sources.name: CNBC Technology
sources.title: Nvidia's Colette Kress confronts key questions in first earnings report since Jensen Huang’s exit
sources.text: Days after Jensen Huang's abrupt departure from the chipmaker he founded 33 years ago, Nvidia interim CEO Colette Kress will now face intense questions about what comes next. Nvidia is scheduled to report quarterly earnings after the close on Tuesday. While the company is again expected to show explosive growth as the key infrastructure provider to the artificial intelligence boom, Kress and her team will likely be forced to answer questions on chip sales to China, the risks tied to deals with neoclouds and what comes next under new leadership. Huang resigned Thursday, but Nvidia's legions of customers, partners and investors still rely on the company to continue shipping large quantities of graphics processing units and AI systems. Kress, who has been Nvidia's CFO since 2013, was tapped to lead the company while the board searches for a successor. Analysts expect Nvidia to report 91% revenue growth to $109.1 billion, according to LSEG, with $2.47 in earnings per share. Kress, alongside Huang, offered a full-year growth forecast suggesting that the company's historic expansion is poised to continue. They said revenue expansion in fiscal 2028 would be roughly 70% in what Kress, on the last earnings call, described as a "supply constrained outlook." "What would be good for them to do is reiterate that and confirm that is still intact, if they have the ability," said Bloomberg Intelligence analyst Kunjan Sobhani. But Kress has to do far more than just put up numbers. The stock has dropped for six straight weeks, the longest losing streak since 2012, pushing the company's market cap down by $1.7 trillion. Here are some key issues Kress has to address: Huang's public downfall began in October, when The New York Times reported that American intelligence agencies were surveilling a woman named Alice Huang, who was close with the former CEO, believing she was a Chinese intelligence asset. The report alleged that Alice Huang was helping smuggle Nvidia's premium chips into China, violating U.S. export controls. An Nvidia spokesperson pushed back on the report saying, "We're confident that if the U.S. government believes that any person is a threat to American industry, it would let us know." Nvidia has also insisted that it gets essentially no data center sales from China, consistent with how it reports sales in its recent Securities and Exchange Commission filings. But Jensen Huang's romantic ties to Alice Huang, a Megaspeed International executive, raised concerns about Nvidia's actual business in China. A big part of Nvidia's sales to Southeast Asia, according to some industry experts, are intended for Chinese companies, either through smuggling the chips to the mainland or by building data centers for Chinese clients in Singapore or Malaysia. In a statement Sunday, a Megaspeed representative said that the cloud provider is conducting a thorough internal investigation, and that Alice Huang left the company in 2025. "Megaspeed designs and maintains its global operational and supply-chain control frameworks to comply with all applicable laws and regulatory regimes, including United States export control requirements and local jurisdiction rules in every market where we operate," Megaspeed said in the statement. Culper Research, a short selling research firm that published a note on Nvidia's "China problem" in May, alleges that 20% of Nvidia's fiscal 2026 compute revenue was "driven by China." Nvidia has denied any diversion, and said it has no evidence that any such activity has taken place. But that was before last week's scandal. Investors will be listening closely to what Kress says about the market for Nvidia's AI chips. Some analysts expect the government to pursue new rules that would force Nvidia to more closely track its customers and how they plan to use the company's critical technology. Kress might not be able to say much, as politicians in Washington, D.C., are ramping up investigations of Nvidia and calling executives to testify in front of Congress. Sen. Ron Wyden, D-Ore., and Rep. Richard Neal. D-Mass., are probing the administration's approvals for Nvidia chip sales to Chinese companies and asked the Commerce Department to save any communications regarding Nvidia and Jensen Huang. Other representatives are asking law enforcement agencies to look into Huang's tryst with the alleged Chinese intelligence asset. Jensen Huang said he would testify in a closed-door meeting with the chairs of the House Foreign Affairs, China and Intelligence committees. The committees are also looking to meet with current Nvidia executives, including Tim Teter, the general counsel. If government officials are able to prove that Nvidia knew that its Southeast Asian clients like Megaspeed were pass-throughs to Chinese companies, the scandal could grow even deeper. "The real story here should be, did Nvidia know their client?" Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said in an interview with CNBC on Friday. "And was there a robust effort at Nvidia to make sure that there was no leakage and that they were selling to what were obviously pass-through shell companies?" Huang was singular in creating a new class of companies called neoclouds, which competed with Nvidia's hyperscaler customers — Microsoft , Amazon , Google , Oracle and SpaceX — by offering Nvidia compute to smaller AI labs and startups. Last quarter, Huang said the company's neocloud business, which it called ACIE, would drive Nvidia's growth going forward. But Nvidia had a unique relationship to the neoclouds, which are often new or nascent businesses that need upfront capital in order to secure land, power and Nvidia chips. Nvidia has acted as supplier, investor and financier to these companies. Huang was integral in deciding who got chips first and publicly pushed to expand Nvidia's role in financing major data center infrastructure. sources.title: ‘A complete evaporation of confidence’–6 critical things Nvidia, and interim CEO Colette Kress, need to nail on the first Jensen-free earnings call
sources.text: Nobody—not even Nvidia’s board—knows who will lead the new regime at Nvidia now that Jensen Huang is gone . For now, longtime CFO Colette Kress is in the driver’s seat as interim chief, and she’s been handed Atlas’s job of holding up the sky during Nvidia’s fiscal 2027 third quarter results after the bell on Tuesday. Kress has to be the “voice of stability” while she also attempts to get the investment community reoriented to the fundamental issues at Nvidia that impact the business and valuation of the stock, said Melissa Otto, global head of Visible Alpha Research at S&P Global. First and foremost, analysts are still expecting a typically gargantuan quarter, with $109.3 billion in revenue, according to S&P’s Visible Alpha consensus—which is routine for Nvidia and will be mission critical for Kress. The quarterly figure is up about 92% from $57 billion last year, but the number has to be delivered in the right way. Nvidia’s gotten the world used to over performance and now the company needs to sizzle with confidence at one of the most vulnerable moments in its history. “There’s a complete evaporation of confidence at the moment, and there’s so much uncertainty around a lot of qualitative issues,” said Otto. “The narrative needs to come back to fundamentals. How is the business doing? Is it achieving what it said it’s going to achieve?” Nvidia’s stock is down 20% since the company’s last quarterly earnings on August 26, losing roughly half a trillion dollars in market cap, amid a broader selloff in AI and related tech stocks that have since rallied. Tuesday could be a moment for Nvidia to make its case (or at least, its first impression) as a post-Jensen business. Or it could be a bloodbath. Here are six key things to pay attention on Nvidia’s earnings conference call. Nvidia told investors in August to expect third-quarter revenue of $108 billion, plus or minus 2%, which puts us in the range of about $105.8 billion to $110.2 billion. That outlook assumed no data center compute revenue from China. Visible Alpha consensus sits at $109.3 billion with earnings of $2.47 per share. The data center segment—Nvidia’s crown jewel—is expected to deliver $101.8 billion of the topline total, with estimates ranging from $99.7 billion to $110.8 billion. Nvidia’s third quarter ended in late October, which means the results were not affected by Huang’s ouster. Still, any signs of weakness in the business during Huang’s final days at the helm would likely add even more uncertainty to the company’s prospects. Jay Woods, chief market strategist at Freedom Capital Markets, wrote in commentary that the earnings report “will be a major referendum on the AI trade following its leadership shake-up, particularly its outlook for demand, margins and financial commitments.” Colossal results “won’t resolve the questions surrounding Jensen’s departure,” he wrote. This is Otto’s top issue. “Do they maintain their guidance for next year?” she said. “If that’s not the case, then there’s going to be some volatility.” That’s putting it lightly. In August, Kress said Nvidia’s preliminary expectation was for revenue to grow about 70% in fiscal 2028 (roughly equivalent to calendar 2027), with supply remaining a bottleneck at least through the end of next year. At the time, Huang said Nvidia had never guided financial figures a year in advance, but with demand running well above 70%, he felt confident about it. The true test will be whether that confidence outlives his ouster. “It is the case that we’ve never forecasted or never guided to a year in advance,” said Huang at the time. “And even though our demand is much greater than 70%, our supply allows us to confidently deliver 70%.” That means $699.2 billion in fiscal 2028 revenue, if Huang’s confidence holds up, according to Visible Alpha’s revenue consensus. In the official announcement of Huang’s resignation last week, Nvidia’s newly installed board chair, Harvey Jones, said the company expects “operations, customer commitments and product roadmap to continue without interruption.” We’ll see. For now, it’s Kress and the board has said it will consider internal and external candidates to replace Huang , whether that’s one person, or a sharing of power in multiple new roles. Otto called the leadership transition “essentially a regime change” and said investors want to hear what comes next. “What changes might be made and how might this affect their existing strategy?” she said. There are also constituencies, mainly other tech founders, who want to see Huang return to his CEO role . Portfolio managers don’t love holding stock that tanks, especially a stock that has been such a rocket ship: Nvidia shares have surged more than 1,300% since ChatGPT’s late 2022 launch. “For a company that spent 33 years under one CEO, this is about more than beating expectations,” Woods wrote. “Nvidia now needs to show that the business can continue delivering without the man who built it.” Giuseppe Sette, cofounder and president of Reflexivity, wrote in commentary that a reinstatement “would most likely trigger a sharp, immediate relief rally,” but on a “less durable and more volatile path than the classic founder-return analogues, since this is a scandal-driven exit rather than a strategy-driven one.” Nvidia has become an important financial backer of its customers , through direct investments and guarantees to backstop debt, with neocloud companies ranking among the biggest beneficiaries. Total future commitments, spread over the next five fiscal years and thereafter, amount to $366 billion, with $120 billion falling in the remainder of fiscal 2027, which ends in late January. Supply and capacity makes up $279 billion of that total, up from $119 billion the quarter before. stories.title: Sam Altman on Nvidia without Jensen Huang: The industry will be ‘fine’
stories.summary: OpenAI CEO Sam Altman acknowledged the special role Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang has played in the AI boom, but ultimately thinks the industry will be “fine” without him at the helm.

sources.name: TechCrunch AI
sources.title: Sam Altman on Nvidia without Jensen Huang: The industry will be ‘fine’
sources.text: OpenAI CEO Sam Altman says the AI industry will be “fine” without Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang at the helm, even as he acknowledged the special role Huang has played in the AI boom. Huang resigned last week from Nvidia after admitting to having an affair with an alleged Chinese spy. Altman made his first public comments about Huang’s departure on Monday at Semafor’s Silicon Valley & The World event, where he also discussed topics ranging from data center pushback to recursive self-improvement. Numerous executives and members of the AI industry have argued for Nvidia to reinstate Huang, including Elon Musk and Epic Games chief executive Tim Sweeney, who were among the signatories in a public letter. Many fear that Huang’s departure may cause Nvidia to rethink the enormous financial risks it has taken that have fueled the AI boom. Huang is also reportedly setting up a “war room” of Silicon Valley executives to lobby for his return. When asked whether he thought Huang should return to the company, Altman said: “I don’t think I know enough to answer that question.” He expressed empathy for Huang’s situation, citing his own ousting from OpenAI in 2023 after board members accused him of withholding information. “It’s hard to imagine the AI revolution without Jensen and the company he has built,” Altman said, adding that he sees Huang as a hero, and that “heroes have flaws.” OpenAI and Nvidia have had a close relationship for the last decade, one that has evolved from a simple chip supplier-customer relationship into a potentially circular financing arrangement, in which Nvidia’s money helps fund purchases of its own chips. Most recently, Nvidia agreed to provide a guarantee of up to $105 billion backing OpenAI’s Ohio data center project. That’s just one of many such circular deals Nvidia has made to bankroll the AI boom while fueling demand for its own chips. Altman said he’s not worried that the Bank of Nvidia will dry up. “Nvidia is, like, a behemoth of a company,” he said. “I think people still trust their guarantees very much.” Altman acknowledged the “ambition” Huang brought to the industry, the scale of which “has been quite important.” But he didn’t go so far as to agree with the many who worry about ripple effects from Huang’s departure. “I think there’s so much demand, and it’s so clear that AI is real, and people want to use it, and the revenues and demand are growing so strongly that I think the industry will be fine,” Altman said. “But again, I think Jensen has played this extremely special and valuable role as someone to really drive things forward with great ambition.” When you purchase through links in our articles, we may earn a small commission . This doesn’t affect our editorial independence. Rebecca Bellan is a senior reporter at TechCrunch where she covers the business, policy, and emerging trends shaping artificial intelligence. Her work has also appeared in Forbes, Bloomberg, The Atlantic, The Daily Beast, and other publications. sources.title: Sam Altman diz que indústria de IA ficará bem sem Jensen Huang na Nvidia
sources.text: O CEO da OpenAI, Sam Altman, acredita que a indústria de inteligência artificial (IA) continuará avançando mesmo sem Jensen Huang no comando da Nvidia . Apesar de reconhecer a importância do executivo para o desenvolvimento do setor, ele afirmou que a demanda por IA é forte o suficiente para manter o mercado em expansão. As declarações foram feitas nesta segunda-feira (16), durante o evento Semafor’s Silicon Valley & The World . Foi a primeira vez que Altman comentou publicamente a saída de Huang da fabricante de chips, após o executivo deixar o cargo de CEO na semana passada. Questionado sobre a possibilidade de o fundador retornar à liderança da Nvidia, Altman evitou tomar partido. “Não acho que eu saiba o suficiente para responder a essa pergunta”, afirmou. A declaração de Altman também chama atenção pela relação comercial entre as duas empresas. A Nvidia é uma das principais fornecedoras de chips utilizados no desenvolvimento e na operação de sistemas de IA da OpenAI. Mais recentemente, a fabricante concordou em oferecer garantias de até US$ 105 bilhões (cerca de R$ 560 bilhões) para respaldar o projeto de data center da OpenAI em Ohio. O acordo faz parte de relação financeira mais complexa entre as companhias. A Nvidia investe no crescimento do mercado de IA e, ao mesmo tempo, ajuda a financiar empresas que compram seus próprios chips. Questionado sobre a possibilidade de a saída de Huang afetar esse tipo de financiamento, Altman disse não estar preocupado. Segundo ele, a Nvidia é uma empresa gigantesca e suas garantias continuam inspirando confiança no mercado. Altman reconheceu que a ambição de Huang e sua capacidade de impulsionar grandes projetos tiveram papel especialmente importante na expansão da IA. Ainda assim, o executivo acredita que o mercado não sofrerá consequências significativas com a saída do fundador da Nvidia. “Há tanta demanda, está tão claro que a IA é real, que as pessoas querem usá-la, e as receitas e a demanda estão crescendo tão fortemente que acredito que a indústria ficará bem”, afirmou. A avaliação contrasta com as preocupações de parte do mercado de tecnologia, que teme que a saída de Huang leve a Nvidia a rever os riscos financeiros assumidos para sustentar a expansão da infraestrutura de IA. Por enquanto, Altman prefere não opinar sobre o futuro do executivo na fabricante de chips. Sua avaliação é que, apesar da importância de Huang, o crescimento da IA não depende exclusivamente de sua permanência no comando da companhia. Rodrigo Mozelli é jornalista formado pela Universidade Metodista de São Paulo (UMESP) e, atualmente, é redator do Olhar Digital.

stories.title: Nvidia stock falls as investors price in fallout from Jensen Huang's resignation
stories.summary: Nvidia's stock continued to slide on Monday following the resignation of CEO Jensen Huang.

sources.name: CNBC Technology
sources.title: Nvidia stock falls as investors price in fallout from Jensen Huang's resignation
sources.text: Nvidia 's stock slid 4.12% Monday in the wake of CEO Jensen Huang 's resignation , leading a broader chipmaker selloff after the chip giant lost hundreds of billions in market cap last week. The continued decline since Huang's resignation brought Nvidia's stock to its lowest close since July 1, 2025. Huang resigned from Nvidia, the company's board announced on Thursday, after mounting scrutiny following reports that he had a relationship with a woman believed to be a Chinese spy. Huang told employees he had an affair in an email on Nov. 8. It was later reported that Huang had romantic relationships with two Nvidia employees. Nvidia did not immediately respond to CNBC's request for comment on Friday. An online petition calling for Huang's reinstatement as Nvidia CEO has drawn more than 170,000 signatures , as prominent tech executives, including Elon Musk , rallied behind him. A source familiar with the matter told CNBC, however, that Nvidia's board of directors is not considering bringing back Huang. Meanwhile, U.S. lawmakers are pushing to launch comprehensive investigations into the scandal. Huang cofounded Nvidia in 1993 and led the company through its meteoric rise to becoming the world's most valuable company, with its AI chips underpinning the technology's boom. Nvidia appointed longtime finance chief Colette Kress as interim CEO and said its board would consider both internal and external candidates in its search for a permanent successor. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent on Sunday called for a "dramatic shakeup" at Nvidia, adding that the board should look outside the company for its next chief executive. He also suggested other Nvidia executives should face scrutiny over the chip giant's compliance with U.S. export controls. — CNBC's Caleigh Keating contributed to this report.

sources.name: Wired AI
sources.title: Nvidia Was Already in Trouble Before the Jensen Huang Mess
sources.text: Nvidia played a key role enabling the AI gold rush thanks in large part to its recently ousted CEO Jensen Huang . Huang was a master of foreseeing technological changes , investing in chips to train AI earlier than most. But just as he’s leaving , the company has a growing list of competitors with a range of new, advanced technology breathing down its neck. For Nvidia , where CFO Colette Kress has now taken the reins, the timing isn’t great. “Everything sold today was designed two to three years ago,” says the CEO of a large AI company, who spoke to WIRED on condition of anonymity to avoid hurting business relationships. Kress, or whoever replaces her permanently, will have to chart the course that the chip industry will take two years from now, the CEO says. Already, competitors have started to move in. Nvidia dominates the market for AI accelerators, capturing 80 percent of sales, according to Silicon Analysis. Longtime nemesis AMD is now making a concerted effort to build competitive AI chips. Its share of the market has crept up from just two percent in 2022 to between 7 and 10 percent in 2026. Big US cloud players—Google, Amazon, and Microsoft—are all developing more specialized chips to power the training and serving of AI models. Each has seen similar gains. These companies are designing their own silicon to reduce costs and to gain some independence from Nvidia. Several startups now offer more specialized chips that promise improvements over Nvidia’s core products. Cerebras, for instance, sells giant ones meant to power giant AI models. AMD recently bought Taalas, a company that burns models’ weights into silicon to make computations ultra efficient. Using these chips requires rewriting a lot of code, however, to make them work with cutting-edge AI models. Patrick Moorhead, chief analyst at MoorInStrat, a company that tracks the chip industry, says the rise of AI agents makes inference, or running models that have already been trained, more important. That’s an area where Nvidia has less of an edge compared to cloud hyperscalers and startups. Nvidia did, however, acquire a startup making specialized chips, called Groq, in December of 2025. And because of the rise in AI assistants and agents, there’s also growing demand for general purpose central processing units (CPUs), Moorhead said, an area where Nvidia barely competes. Nvidia still maintains a huge lead in AI thanks to Huang’s foresight. Huang cofounded the company in 1993 to design graphics chips for PCs. In the mid-2010s, he saw the promise of AI. He funded academic research on the topic, developed software to support AI engineering, and gave hardware to labs and startups. In 2022, ChatGPT took AI mainstream and sales of Nvidia chips skyrocketed. The company’s revenue went from $26.91 billion in January 2022 to $215.94 billion in January 2026. The challenges it faces may not be existential—but they do add up, especially on a global scale. While Nvidia’s fortunes have risen in the US, they have declined in the world’s other big market for AI: China. Washington is trying to restrict access to its most advanced chips, while Beijing is trying to develop its own chip industry. Nvidia is not allowed to sell its most powerful chips in China, but it can sell previous generations. Sales of these chips as well as non AI chips doubled over the past year, but China now accounts for only eight percent of the company’s overall revenue, compared with 20 percent in 2024, according to its fillings. It remains unclear how many chips exported to other countries may either end up in China or end up being used remotely by Chinese firms. Huawei, a Chinese tech giant targeted with US sanctions for several years, has developed new kinds of supercomputers that harness many more chips than usual to train and run AI models. Some Chinese AI companies, such as Z.ai, which makes one of the world’s best open source models, say they’ve trained their models entirely using Huawei’s chips. If Chinese open-weight models gain traction in other countries, it could create a market for Chinese chips elsewhere. Huang’s dealings with China played a major role in his downfall. He had a romantic relationship with Huang Le, also known as Alice Huang, a Chinese executive at a Singaporean company called Megaspeed who the US government suspects of being an asset of China’s Ministry of State Security. Megaspeed and its subsidiaries have reportedly imported between $4.6 and $7.5 billion Nvidia chips into southeast Asia. Reports suggest that the company may have provided access to the chips to Chinese AI firms. Babak Minovi, a senior analyst at the Eurasia Group, a consultancy that focuses on technology and geopolitics, says Huang was right to point out that cutting off access to China would empower domestic rivals. “Huang was taking a pragmatic line, and he knows competition,” he says. Even in markets that it dominates, Nvidia may turn out to be a victim of its own success. The AI models built using Nvidia’s chip are automating the very elements of coding, data analysis, and scientific research that help design chips. Most chip design firms use specialized AI models to arrange components on processors—something that traditionally required deep engineering expertise and experience. And both OpenAI and Anthropic have recently touted the ability of their newest models to design electronics from scratch. Moorhead says the shift towards AI chip design may not pose a huge threat to Nvidia because it’s riding the same wave. “They have access to AI too,” he notes. But Moorhead says the way AI models can now quickly rewrite code to run on different hardware may prove a problem. For years, Nvidia has attracted developers by providing software that makes it easy to write programs and build models for its silicon. Its Compute Unified Device Architecture, or CUDA, has long been seen as a moat to ensure AI companies continue to rely on Nvidia chips. But AI models are now so good at read

stories.title: How we make Together AI easy for coding agents to use
stories.summary: We built agent evals to test how effective coding agents are at using Together AI. Small fixes to our docs, skills, and API errors lifted task completion rate from 75% to 97%.

sources.name: Together AI
sources.title: How we make Together AI easy for coding agents to use
sources.text: Earlier this year, we started seeing more and more devs using coding agents to build with Together AI. It’s not hard to see why: It might take days or even weeks for a developer to wire up an app for production inference by hand, especially if they’re new to the platform. But for an agent using our SDK and CLI, it only takes a few minutes—at least in theory. In practice, we had no idea whether the agents pointed at our platform were able to work with Together efficiently, or if they were hitting obstacles, going down rabbit holes or failing outright, and wasting tokens in the process. As devs delegate more of their work to agents, developer experience (DX) is increasingly becoming synonymous with agent experience (AX). The easier your software is for agents to use, the easier it is for devs to build it into their own products and workflows. GitHub is a textbook example of great AX: activity on the platform has tripled in the past year, with agents opening about 40% of all PRs in 2026 (and, we’re willing to bet, writing a lot more than 40% of the lines of code across all commits). This is thanks to GitHub’s phenomenal API, CLI, and docs, all of which make it exceptionally easy for agents to use. (This writer was not even aware GitHub had a CLI until agents started using it for him, and now he probably uses it 1000+ times a day). To improve our AX at Together AI, we needed a way to measure how agent-ready our platform actually was. In this post, we’ll walk through how we run agent evals, two problems they uncovered and how we fixed them, and what we’ve learned. Before we could start evaluating, we needed to know what agents were actually being asked to do … so we could, y’know, figure out if they could do those things. We started building a list of common tasks that developers tackle on Together, like running a batch inference job, building a voice agent, or managing autoscaling for an inference endpoint. By task, we really just mean a prompt, something you’d tell an agent to do—for example: The prompt asks for both availability and pricing, without mentioning that these details live in two different places. This is realistic, as the average user probably doesn’t know up front where each piece of information lives, which could easily trip up both humans and agents. After building our list of tasks, we run each one of them three ways: Each full evaluation runs every task against each agent configuration using three models, with two attempts at each task—so six attempts per task for each config, as shown here for our run on September 30th: When we started building our evals, we ran everything by hand: open a new terminal, paste a prompt into Claude Code, let the agent do its thing (or fail to do its thing), and repeat for each configuration. It was manual and tedious, so once we figured out the shape of the system we wanted, we started automating it. Now we run each agent in a Together sandbox so they don’t interfere with our local environment or each other. GitHub Actions handles setup, starts the agent, cleans up afterward, and saves the results, while a proxy handles the agent's requests to the Together API and records the activity, so we can see which endpoints the agent calls and what comes back. After a run finishes, an LLM judge reviews the task prompt and the recorded session, then assigns one of three verdicts: Failed and incomplete verdicts don’t necessarily tell us whether the problem was with the agent, the API, or missing evidence. They just tell us where to start looking. We investigate passing runs too. An agent can often work around confusing responses and still finish, and those recoveries show us what to fix to improve token efficiency. To make that review practical, we built a results viewer that compares how different models and configs performed. For each run, it shows the prompt, the tools the agent used, the responses it got back, and any API activity: Remember the GPU cluster task from earlier? Seems pretty simple, but when we ran our evals early last summer, Sonnet 4.6 passed only 4 of 15 attempts at this task, even with skills enabled. Our post-mortem revealed the same pattern in the failed runs: Sonnet treated the sample output in our CLI reference, which listed a single region and two GPU types, as if it were the live inventory. It also skipped the regions lookup and named what it thought was the cheapest option without ever checking the pricing page. The problems were on our end. First, the sample output wasn’t properly labeled, so nothing told the agent to run the command to retrieve the relevant data. Second, our skill file linked to the GPU clusters marketing page rather than the pricing table, so Sonnet opened the marketing page, didn’t see any real prices, and just made a best-effort guess at the cheapest GPU available. More capable models were able to work around the issue. In that same period, Opus 4.8 passed 13 of 14 attempts using the same config. According to the transcript, it noticed that the list_regions response didn't include prices, so it kept searching until it found them in our docs. This is why it’s crucial to test your product with less capable models; if we had only tested with Opus, it would have taken us much longer to find the gap. To fix it, we isolated the failure by pulling the GPU clusters skill out of the full skill package, and wrote a narrower prompt that reproduced only this issue. It failed every time when tested against the old skill file, so we had reliable repro steps (use the old skill), and an easy way to test each new version (update the skill). We went through several iterations until we landed on a small change: two new sentences in the skill that point the agent to the pricing table, and explain how to use it with the live regions API: After this change, the task passed 100% of the time for all models we tested using the skill-enabled config. The same GPU task also turned up a problem in our API. In a recent baseline run,

sources.title: TokenEconomizer: Learning from Experience to Make AI Coding Agents More Efficient
sources.text: By Aaron J. Li , Research Intern Weijia Xu , Senior Researcher Chandan Singh , Staff Research Scientist Zixiao Chen Jeevana Priya Inala , Senior Researcher Bin Yu , Professor Ion Stoica , Professor Michel Galley , Senior Principal Research Manager Jianfeng Gao , Technical Fellow & Corporate Vice President AI coding agents are increasingly helping developers fix bugs and build features largely on their own, but every interaction with their models consumes tokens. In each session , an agent sends instructions, tool descriptions, and session history to its model. Most efforts to reduce this cost focus on individual tasks. Yet developers return to the same repositories, giving agents an opportunity to learn from previous work. Without that learning, an agent may repeatedly rediscover how to run tests, load tools it never uses, or spend dozens of turns revisiting the same error. In our paper, TokenEconomizer: Experience-Driven Black-Box Cost Control for Coding Agents , we ask a simple question: can experience in a repository help an agent solve future tasks more efficiently? TokenEconomizer, an open-source plugin from UC Berkeley, Microsoft Research, and Microsoft Security, turns completed sessions into guidance for subsequent ones. It reduces waste without changing the agent or its underlying model, so developers can use it alongside the coding agents they already rely on. We first profiled Claude Code on 60 tasks from SWE-Bench, a benchmark of real bug fixes in open-source Python projects, running each repository’s tasks in sequence. Three kinds of waste recurred: We also tested three popular open-source plugins, each built around a fixed cost-saving strategy. Each lowered costs in some repositories but not others. Together, these findings suggest that effective cost control must adapt to the repository, rather than apply the same strategy everywhere. Join us for a continuous exchange of ideas about research in the era of general AI. Watch the latest episodes on demand. After each session, TokenEconomizer reads the session’s log and updates what it knows about the repository. It then acts through three mechanisms, using only interfaces the agent already provides, as illustrated in Figure 2. Micro-skills capture repository-specific knowledge in one-line notes. TokenEconomizer identifies recurring patterns across sessions and proposes corresponding notes. They are added to the agent’s starting context only after several sessions have confirmed the pattern, and retires the note if later evidence contradicts it. Tool pruning removes tools that repository history suggests the agent is unlikely to use , while always retaining core tools for running commands and editing files. Removed tools can be restored if needed. Failure-loop intervention watches for an agent that keeps hitting the same failure. A judge model decides whether the agent is truly stuck or still making progress. If it is stuck, the agent gets a short note suggesting a different approach. In the open-source plugin, if the agent is still stuck after the note, TokenEconomizer alerts the developer rather than stopping the work itself. The controller is designed to revise its decisions as new evidence arrives. Reported savings also account for the cost of TokenEconomizer’s own model calls. We evaluated TokenEconomizer on 277 SWE-Bench tasks from six repositories, using five different AI coding agent and model combinations. For each repository, TokenEconomizer started with no prior session history. TokenEconomizer lowered the average cost by 18.4–30.9%, as shown in Figure 3, and saved the most in all 30 repository-combination pairs without performance loss. By contrast, lowering the model’s reasoning effort saved similar or larger amounts but led to substantial performance degradation. Savings grow as experience accumulates. Early tasks can cost more while TokenEconomizer learns, but cumulative costs fell below the default in every repository by the sixth task, shown inFigure 4. Each mechanism contributes savings on its own, and combining all three delivers the largest reduction. The savings also carried over to sequential web development, with costs 16.0–21.2% lower on Web-Bench. On security auditing, where every task is in a new repository, costs were 6.4–19.6% lower. TokenEconomizer opens a path toward coding agents that learn not only how to solve tasks, but also how to spend computation more effectively. Its lightweight controller shows how experience can improve efficiency without changing the underlying agent or model. The open-source plugin makes these directions accessible to developers and researchers. It is designed to run alongside existing AI coding agents without modifying their underlying models, requires no API key of its own, and keeps what it learns on the developer’s machine. We invite the community to use it as a starting point for exploring agents that become more resourceful with experience, adapting how they work, as well as what they know. Technical Fellow & Corporate Vice President

stories.title: Hugging Face and OpenRouter join forces to make open-weight models easy to run

sources.name: Hugging Face
sources.title: Hugging Face and OpenRouter join forces to make open-weight models easy to run
sources.text: Hugging Face and OpenRouter are teaming up to make open-weight models easy to run. Every major open-weight release is already being published on the Hugging Face Hub, and OpenRouter serves those models at scale, routing each request across 80+ providers based on live measurements of each one. Together, every open-weight model on the Hub that a provider serves can be called with your Hugging Face token, through the same API, with the best provider picked for each request. Today, we are switching Inference Providers from our own custom router to OpenRouter's. Requests made to language models now go through OpenRouter, which picks the best provider for each call based on live price, speed and reliability, and retries on another provider if the first one fails. Your code stays the same. The router supports OpenAI's Chat Completions and Responses APIs and Anthropic's Messages API for every chat model, whatever the provider behind it. Pick your coding agent or SDK and a model, then copy the steps, or copy the whole setup as a prompt for your agent: Setup guides for Claude Code , Codex , OpenCode , Pi and Hermes Agent The same Hugging Face token also gives you storage with Storage Buckets , compute with Jobs and dedicated inference with Inference Endpoints . PRO, Team and Enterprise plans include monthly credits for compute and inference. On OpenRouter, open-weight models went from 26.8% of the tokens served in October 2025 to 71.7% at the end of September 2026, after peaking at 77.5% in July ( OpenRouter, October 2026 ). Over the same period, weekly open-weight volume grew more than 60-fold, against almost tenfold for closed models. This week, the most used model on OpenRouter is an open-weight one, DeepSeek V4.1 Flash 1017, with 59.2 trillion tokens ( rankings ). Open-weight models cost about four times less on average: $0.28 per million input tokens and $1.62 per million output tokens, against $1.27 and $6.36 for closed models. The best open-weight models still trail the best proprietary ones on the hardest benchmarks. On the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index , Kimi K3.1 Pro, the best open-weight model, scores 46 against 65 for Claude Fable 5.2, at about a seventh of the cost per task ($3.68 against $26.54). For a lot of workloads, that trade-off is worth it. OpenRouter serves more than 800 trillion tokens a month to over 10 million users, across 600+ models from 80+ providers. Its routing is based on live measurements of every provider across that traffic. OpenRouter recently rebuilt its provider routing : instead of only looking at the lowest list price, it sends each request to the provider with the best mix of price, speed and reliability. When a provider slows down or starts failing, traffic moves away from it until it recovers, and a failed try is retried on the next best provider inside the same call. In OpenRouter's measurements, the new routing cut capacity errors by 46% and improved time to first token by 16.9% and throughput by 16.3%. Before, Inference Providers picked one provider for your request and returned its error if it failed. Now, the request is retried on another provider. You can still choose a policy or a provider with a suffix on the model id: Routing is also cache-aware: a conversation stays on the provider that holds its prompt cache. To make it explicit, send a stable UUID per conversation in the X-HF-Session-Id header (see the prompt caching guide ). Pricing doesn't change: you pay the provider's price on your Hugging Face bill, and Hugging Face doesn't add a markup on top of it. PRO users get $2 of credits every month, and Team and Enterprise organizations get $2 per seat. See Pricing and Billing for the details. Image, video, and audio generation continue to work exactly as before, directly through Hugging Face Inference Providers without going through OpenRouter. You can keep using the same token and API, and access tens of thousands of LoRAs . On model pages, you can chat with the model right away in the widget. Two new tabs show what's behind it: Providers lists every provider OpenRouter can route the model to, with its input and output price, speed and uptime over the last 24 hours, and Metrics shows the best price, throughput, time to first token, context length and uptime among them: Your usage overview breaks your spend down by the provider each request went to: In your settings , you can turn off any provider you don't want: the router never sends your requests there. Organizations have the same settings, and they apply to every request billed to the organization. Requests to language models now go through OpenRouter and are billed to your Hugging Face account or organization, so you can no longer use your own API key for a provider with these models. You can still pick a provider with a suffix on the model id ( model:provider ) or turn providers off in your settings, and your code stays the same. Custom keys for image and video providers keep working. This is the first step of our partnership with OpenRouter. Next: Try a model , or read the Inference Providers docs to get started.

sources.name: Roboflow
sources.title: OpenRouter Vision Models in Roboflow
sources.text: To compare OpenRouter vision models, run them side by side on your own images in Roboflow Workflows: connect one image to several OpenRouter blocks, switch models by changing the model ID, and compare answers, token counts, and response time in a single run. Add RF-DETR to detect and crop objects before the VLM call, then deploy the same pipeline through the Serverless API or on live video streams. Testing a vision-language model from another provider often means changing your code before you can try it on an image. OpenRouter gives you access to hundreds of models through one API. In Roboflow Workflows , you can run models in a visual pipeline. We'll build a workflow that sends the same image to three vision models and see how their answers differ. We'll also compare response times and check the input and output token counts. OpenRouter offers more than 300 models from different providers. Some of these are vision-language models (VLMs) , which accept images along with text prompts to analyze visual content. For example, a VLM can read text on a product package or identify its product category. It can also describe the objects in a scene. The accuracy of the result depends on the model and the image. Working with providers separately means managing different API keys and request formats. You could also need to change how your code reads their responses. Providers can handle failed requests differently, which affects how you write retry logic. OpenRouter gives you a common way to send requests to supported models. You can switch between vision models by changing the model ID instead of rewriting the integration. Roboflow Workflows is a visual editor where you can connect computer vision models with processing steps. Start by creating a new Workflow in your Roboflow workspace with an image input. Add the OpenRouter block to the pipeline and connect it to the image input. Then connect the OpenRouter block to Outputs to return the model's response. Click the OpenRouter block to open its settings. For this example, I selected Amazon Nova Pro (amazon/nova-pro-v1) in the Model ID field. The prompt tells the model what to look for in the image, such as text printed on product packaging. You can adjust the temperature to control how much responses vary and set max tokens to limit the length of the output. Reasoning effort controls how much reasoning a model uses, if supported. The privacy level setting lets you choose how providers can handle your request data. By default, Roboflow's OpenRouter block uses a Roboflow-managed API key, with usage charged through Roboflow credits. If you want to be billed directly by OpenRouter instead of using Roboflow credits, enter your personal OpenRouter API key in the block's API Key field. Depending on the model, the OpenRouter block can handle open prompts, optical character recognition ( OCR ), visual question answering , short and detailed image captions, single-label and multi-label classification , object detection, and structured JSON answers. I tested three of these tasks with Amazon Nova Pro using a fictional Northfield Pantry granola package. I uploaded the packaging image and asked the model to read the printed text. It correctly recognized the product name, ingredients, 340 g weight, lot code NP-2047, and best-before date 2027-08-14. For classification, I provided a list of categories and possible labels. The model selected breakfast cereal as the primary category. It also assigned breakfast food, contains almonds, and honey-flavored as additional labels. Single-label classification selects one category, while multi-label classification can return several. I also asked the model to extract product_name, brand, and quantity. It returned Honey Almond Granola, Northfield Pantry, and 340 g in a JSON-formatted string. These values could be used to fill product details in an inventory system. To compare three vision models, I used the same image and prompt for each one. This let me compare their answers and token usage under similar conditions. I reused the fictional Northfield Pantry granola package image. It has a clear product name and several printed details that the models can read. I created a new Workflow with one image input and three OpenRouter blocks. Each block connects directly to the same image input, allowing the models to process it independently. Connect each model's response and token counts to Outputs. Give each output a separate name so the results are easy to identify. For this comparison, I selected three vision models from different providers: All three blocks used Open Prompt, a temperature of 0.1, and a maximum of 300 output tokens. I kept the Roboflow-managed API key and the No data collection privacy setting. Reasoning effort was disabled. This keeps the task consistent while changing the model. I uploaded the packaging image and ran the Workflow. The Output panel showed the response from each model, along with its input and output token counts. To measure response time, each model was tested separately three times using the same image and prompt. The median Workflow processing time was calculated for each model. These results include Workflow overhead because the OpenRouter blocks do not return individual model latency. The following table shows the results from the three-model Workflow and the separate timing tests. All three models correctly extracted the seven fields from the packaging image. The main differences were in token usage and processing time. DeepSeek used the fewest input tokens, while Cohere used the most. Cohere also had the shortest median Workflow processing time, although the differences between the models were small. These results come from a single image and don't show which model performs best overall. Testing more images with different levels of difficulty would help determine that. Token counts can help estimate usage costs, which depend on each model's pricing. RF-DETR (opens in a new tab) , Roboflow's
